overview: Testing data pipelines in CI means automatically verifying, on every code change, that your extract, transform, and load logic is correct, that it runs against realistic infrastructure, and that the data it produces meets agreed quality contracts before anything reaches production.

Unlike testing a stateless web service, data pipeline testing has two dimensions: testing the code (does the transformation compute the right result?) and testing the data (are row counts, schemas, nulls, and business rules within expected bounds?). A mature CI setup covers both.

The practical goal engineers aim for is a fast, layered test suite - unit tests for pure functions, integration tests against a real containerized database, data-quality assertions with dbt or Great Expectations, and a few end-to-end runs in a throwaway environment - all wired into GitHub Actions so a red pipeline blocks the merge.
learningObjectives: Apply the data pipeline testing pyramid: many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests against a real containerized warehouse, focused data-quality assertions, and a small number of end-to-end tests.
Build reliable, deterministic tests using pytest fixtures, factory and golden/snapshot data, mocking of external systems, and testcontainers/Docker Compose to run a real Postgres or DuckDB in CI.
Orchestrate the whole suite in GitHub Actions with matrix builds, caching, ephemeral per-PR warehouse schemas, dbt build in a sandbox, published test reports, and merge gating.
coreConcept.formalDefinition: Testing data pipelines in CI is the discipline of running an automated, layered suite of correctness and data-quality checks against every code change within a continuous integration system, so that regressions in transformation logic, schema, and data quality are caught before merge and deploy. It spans code tests (unit tests of pure transform functions, integration tests exercising real database interactions) and data tests (assertions on schema, row counts, uniqueness, referential integrity, freshness, and business rules), executed against reproducible infrastructure - typically ephemeral containers or throwaway warehouse schemas provisioned per pull request. Its defining properties are determinism (same input yields the same pass/fail regardless of when or where it runs), isolation (tests do not touch shared production data and clean up after themselves), and speed layering (cheap fast tests run on every push, expensive end-to-end tests run selectively), all gated so a failing check blocks the merge.
coreConcept.simpleExplanation: Think of a pipeline as a factory line that takes raw material (data) and produces a finished product (tables). Testing in CI is the quality-control inspection that runs automatically every time someone changes the machinery. First you check each individual machine part works on its own (unit tests). Then you run the parts together on a small real conveyor belt spun up just for the test (integration tests against a container database). Then you inspect the finished product against a checklist - no missing parts, right count, no duplicates (data-quality tests). Finally you occasionally run one full item end to end. If any inspection fails, the line is stopped and the change is not allowed onto the factory floor until it is fixed.
coreConcept.historicalContext: Early data pipelines were tested manually or not at all - engineers ran a script and eyeballed the output. As ETL moved into code, unit testing frameworks (pytest, released 2004 and dominant by the mid-2010s) let teams test transform functions in isolation, but connecting to real databases in tests remained painful and flaky. The testcontainers library (Java 2015, Python port maturing around 2019-2021) made it practical to boot a real Postgres in a test and tear it down afterward. In parallel, the analytics-engineering movement - dbt (launched 2016) - popularized data tests as first-class artifacts (schema/data tests, and later unit tests for models in dbt 1.8, 2024). Great Expectations (2018) and Soda brought declarative data-quality assertions and data contracts. GitHub Actions (2019) then made it cheap to run all of this on every pull request, and ephemeral per-PR warehouse schemas (Slim CI in dbt) became the standard for testing changed models without rebuilding the whole warehouse.

whyItMatters.business: A single bad transformation that ships to production can silently corrupt dashboards, financial reports, and downstream ML features for days before anyone notices; CI testing catches these before merge, protecting revenue-critical decisions and customer trust.
whyItMatters.engineering: Automated, layered tests let engineers refactor pipelines and upgrade dependencies with confidence, because a red check on the pull request tells them exactly what broke instead of discovering it in a 2am production incident.
whyItMatters.scalability: As the number of models, sources, and contributors grows, only automated CI testing scales - manual review cannot verify hundreds of transformations and data contracts, but a matrix of tests on every PR can.
whyItMatters.cost: Catching a defect in CI costs minutes of compute; the same defect in production costs backfills, reprocessing, emergency on-call, and lost analyst time - CI testing is the cheapest place in the lifecycle to find and fix bugs.
whyItMatters.reliability: Data tests on schema, freshness, uniqueness, and business rules turn 'the numbers look wrong' into an explicit, automated contract, so pipelines fail loudly and early rather than delivering plausible-but-wrong data downstream.

coreComponents.name: Unit tests for pure transform functions
coreComponents.definition: Fast, isolated tests (typically pytest) that call a single transformation function with in-memory input and assert on the exact returned output, with no database or network involved.
coreComponents.purpose: To verify the business logic of transformations - filtering, aggregation, deduplication, type casting - correctly and in milliseconds, forming the wide base of the testing pyramid.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Exercise edge cases (nulls, empty input, duplicates, timezone boundaries), pin exact expected outputs, and run on every push to give near-instant feedback on logic regressions.
coreComponents.examples: pytest test_transforms.py::test_dedup_keeps_latest | assert normalize_email(' A@B.com ') == 'a@b.com' | parametrize cases for tax rounding

coreComponents.name: Integration tests against a real containerized database
coreComponents.definition: Tests that spin up a genuine Postgres or DuckDB (via testcontainers or Docker Compose), load fixtures, run the pipeline's SQL or ORM code against it, and assert on the resulting tables.
coreComponents.purpose: To catch bugs that only appear with a real engine - SQL dialect quirks, constraint violations, transaction behavior, type coercion - that mocks and unit tests cannot reveal.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Provision an ephemeral database, apply migrations/DDL, seed representative data, run the real query path, assert on rows, and tear the container down cleanly.
coreComponents.examples: PostgresContainer('postgres:16') | duckdb.connect() with seed parquet | run migrations then assert row counts

coreComponents.name: Data-quality tests and contracts
coreComponents.definition: Declarative assertions on the data itself - not_null, unique, accepted_values, referential integrity, freshness, row-count bounds - expressed as dbt tests, Great Expectations expectations, Soda checks, or schema contracts.
coreComponents.purpose: To enforce an explicit contract about what valid output looks like, so pipelines fail when the data (as opposed to the code) violates expectations.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Validate schema shape and types, key uniqueness and relationships, null/range/enum constraints, freshness, and volume anomalies against defined thresholds, and report violations in CI.
coreComponents.examples: dbt test --select orders | expect_column_values_to_not_be_null('customer_id') | soda scan checks.yml

coreComponents.name: End-to-end tests and CI orchestration
coreComponents.definition: A small number of tests that run the full pipeline (extract -> transform -> load) against a throwaway environment, plus the GitHub Actions workflow that sequences unit, integration, data, and E2E stages, caches dependencies, and gates the merge.
coreComponents.purpose: To verify the whole system wires together correctly and to make the entire suite run automatically on every pull request with clear pass/fail gating.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Provision an ephemeral schema/environment per PR, run the full DAG, assert final outputs, publish test reports, enforce coverage/quality gates, and tear everything down for cost control.
coreComponents.examples: gh workflow: matrix build + cache + dbt build --target ci | upload-artifact test-results | branch protection required check

internalWorking: A unit test imports a transform function and calls it with a small in-memory structure (a list of dicts, a pandas or Polars DataFrame); pytest compares the return value to a hardcoded expected value with 'assert', and because nothing external is touched the test is deterministic and runs in milliseconds - failures point straight at the logic that changed.

An integration test uses testcontainers to start a real database in Docker inside the CI runner; the library pulls the pinned image (e.g. postgres:16), waits for a readiness signal (a log line or successful connection), yields a connection string to the test via a pytest fixture, runs the pipeline's real SQL/DDL against it, and on teardown stops and removes the container so no state leaks between tests.

A data-quality test compiles declarative rules into queries: a dbt 'unique' test becomes a SELECT that groups by the column and returns rows with count > 1, and the test passes only if that query returns zero rows; Great Expectations similarly translates each expectation into a validation over the batch and produces a structured pass/fail result with the offending values.

For dbt in CI, 'dbt build' (or 'dbt build --defer --select state:modified+' in Slim CI) runs models and their tests together into an ephemeral, PR-specific schema in the warehouse; unchanged upstream tables are deferred to the production build via a stored manifest so only changed models and their descendants are rebuilt, keeping the run fast and cheap.

GitHub Actions ties it together: on a pull_request event the workflow checks out the code, restores cached dependencies keyed by a hash of the lockfile, runs each stage as a job (with a matrix expanding Python/warehouse versions into parallel runners), uploads JUnit/HTML test reports as artifacts, and reports each job as a status check - branch protection then blocks merge unless the required checks are green, and a teardown step drops the ephemeral schema.
coreConcept.architectureFlow: developer pushes branch & opens PR -> GitHub Actions triggers on pull_request -> checkout & restore dependency cache -> lint & unit tests (fast, matrix over Python versions) -> integration tests spin up testcontainers Postgres/DuckDB & assert -> provision ephemeral warehouse schema for the PR -> dbt build --target ci (models + data tests in sandbox schema) -> optional end-to-end run of full DAG -> publish JUnit/HTML test reports as artifacts -> required status checks gate merge -> teardown ephemeral schema/containers for cost control
dataFlowWalkthrough: 1. A developer pushes a branch and opens a pull request; the GitHub Actions workflow triggers on the pull_request event and checks out the exact commit under review.
2. The workflow restores the pip/uv and dbt package caches keyed by the lockfile hash, then runs linting and the unit-test job across a matrix of Python versions, giving feedback in under a minute.

3. The integration job uses testcontainers to boot a pinned Postgres (or an in-process DuckDB), applies DDL/migrations, seeds fixture rows, runs the pipeline's real SQL, and asserts on the resulting tables before tearing the container down.

4. A step provisions an ephemeral, PR-scoped schema in the warehouse (e.g. dbt_ci_pr_1234) and runs 'dbt build --target ci', which materializes only changed models and executes their schema/data tests in that isolated sandbox using Slim CI deferral.

5. Test reports (JUnit XML and an HTML summary) are uploaded as artifacts and surfaced on the PR, required status checks block the merge if anything is red, and a final always-run step drops the ephemeral schema and removes containers to control cost.

keyTerminology.meaning: A model prescribing many cheap unit tests at the base, fewer integration tests in the middle, targeted data-quality tests, and a small number of slow end-to-end tests at the top.
keyTerminology.importance: It keeps the suite fast and stable: most feedback comes from milliseconds-fast unit tests, while expensive, flaky-prone E2E tests are kept rare, so CI stays quick and trustworthy.

keyTerminology.meaning: A library that programmatically starts real services (Postgres, Kafka, etc.) in throwaway Docker containers for the duration of a test and tears them down automatically afterward.
keyTerminology.importance: It lets integration tests run against a genuine, pinned database engine in CI - catching dialect and constraint bugs mocks miss - without any shared or manually managed test database.

keyTerminology.meaning: 'dbt test' runs data assertions (unique, not_null, relationships, custom) against models; 'dbt build' runs models and their tests together in dependency order.
keyTerminology.importance: It makes data-quality checks first-class, version-controlled artifacts that run in CI, turning informal expectations about the data into enforced, automated contracts.

keyTerminology.meaning: A short-lived, isolated environment - often a per-PR warehouse schema or a Kubernetes namespace/preview deployment - created for a change and destroyed after tests finish.
keyTerminology.importance: It lets each pull request be tested against real infrastructure without touching production or other PRs, and disciplined teardown keeps warehouse/compute costs from ballooning.

keyTerminology.meaning: A test that compares current output against a stored, reviewed 'golden' reference (e.g. an expected CSV/JSON), failing on any diff and requiring an explicit update to the reference.
keyTerminology.importance: It efficiently guards complex, wide outputs where writing per-field asserts is impractical, making unintended output changes visible and reviewable in the diff.

importantConcepts.concept: Test the code and the data separately
importantConcepts.explanation: Data pipeline reliability has two distinct failure modes that need different tests. Code tests answer 'given this input, does my transformation compute the correct output?' - they are deterministic, use fixed fixtures, and fail when logic regresses. Data tests answer 'is the actual data flowing through the pipeline valid?' - they check nulls, uniqueness, referential integrity, freshness, and volume against a contract, and they can fail even when the code is perfect (because an upstream source changed). Conflating the two leads to gaps: teams with great unit tests still ship silent data corruption because no assertion checked the output data, and teams with only dbt tests miss logic bugs that happen to produce contract-valid but wrong numbers. A mature pipeline has both layers, run in CI.

A CI test that passes today and fails tomorrow with no code change is worse than no test, because teams learn to ignore red builds. The two root causes are non-determinism (tests that depend on the current time, random ordering, network calls to live systems, or shared mutable state) and lack of isolation (tests that read or write a shared database and interfere with each other or with production). The fixes are: freeze time (freezegun) and seed randomness, mock or containerize every external dependency, give each test its own transaction or ephemeral schema, and always tear down. Determinism plus isolation is what makes a red build trustworthy - which is the entire point of gating merges on it.

importantConcepts.concept: Slim CI: test only what changed
importantConcepts.explanation: Rebuilding an entire warehouse of thousands of models on every pull request is slow and expensive, so mature dbt setups use 'Slim CI'. dbt stores a manifest (state) from the last successful production build as an artifact; in CI, 'dbt build --select state:modified+ --defer' compares the PR against that manifest, rebuilds only the modified models and everything downstream of them, and 'defers' unchanged upstream references to the existing production tables instead of rebuilding them. This turns a multi-hour full build into a few-minute targeted build that still exercises the real changes and their blast radius, provisioned into an ephemeral PR schema. It is the key technique that makes warehouse testing in CI economically viable at scale.

variationsAndTypes: **Unit tests:** pytest for Python transforms, dbt unit tests (dbt 1.8+) for model SQL logic with mocked inputs, and SQLGlot-based dialect checks for portable SQL.
**Integration tests:** testcontainers (real Postgres/MySQL/Kafka), Docker Compose services in CI, or an in-process DuckDB/SQLite for a fast, dependency-free relational engine.
**Data-quality tools:** dbt tests (built-in + dbt_utils + dbt_expectations), Great Expectations, Soda Core, Pandera for DataFrame schemas, and Deequ/PyDeequ on Spark.
**Fixtures and reference data:** pytest fixtures, factory_boy/faker for synthetic records, golden/snapshot files, and small seeded CSV/parquet datasets checked into the repo.
**Ephemeral environments:** per-PR warehouse schemas (dbt Slim CI), Kubernetes namespaces, preview deployments, and cloud data sandboxes torn down on merge/close.
**CI platforms:** GitHub Actions (matrix + caching + artifacts), GitLab CI, CircleCI, and Dagster/Airflow-native test harnesses, all serving the same layered strategy.
advantages: **Catches regressions before merge:** a red check on the PR stops broken transformation logic and data-contract violations from ever reaching production.
**Fast, layered feedback:** the pyramid delivers most results from millisecond unit tests, so engineers iterate quickly while heavier tests run in parallel.
**Realistic confidence:** testcontainers and ephemeral warehouse schemas exercise the real engine, catching dialect, constraint, and integration bugs that mocks hide.
**Explicit data contracts:** dbt/Great Expectations assertions turn vague expectations about the data into automated, version-controlled checks that fail loudly.
disadvantages: **Slower pipelines if over-tested:** too many integration/E2E tests or full warehouse rebuilds make CI slow, frustrating developers and inviting skipped checks.
**Fixture and data maintenance:** seed data, golden files, and expectations drift out of date and must be curated, or tests become noisy or falsely green.
**Warehouse cost:** running dbt builds and ephemeral schemas per PR consumes real compute; without Slim CI and teardown, costs escalate quickly.
**Flakiness risk:** container startup timing, network, and non-deterministic data can produce intermittent failures that erode trust in the suite if not controlled.

tradeOffs.whenToUse: Invest in full layered CI testing for any pipeline whose output feeds decisions, dashboards, ML features, or other teams - especially with many contributors and frequent changes, where regressions are costly and manual review cannot scale.
tradeOffs.whenToAvoid: For a one-off exploratory notebook or a throwaway backfill script run once, a full CI test harness is overkill; keep tests lightweight (a few unit tests and a schema check) and skip ephemeral warehouse environments when the data is non-critical and rarely changed.

coreConcept.realWorldAnalogy: Testing a pipeline in CI is like the quality process in a car factory. Individual parts are bench-tested in isolation first - does this specific gear turn correctly (unit tests)? Then subassemblies are tested on a real rig wired up just for the test and dismantled afterward (integration tests on a container database). The finished car goes through an inspection checklist - correct number of doors, no missing bolts, VIN matches (data-quality assertions on schema, counts, uniqueness). A few complete cars are taken for a full test drive (end-to-end tests). And crucially, the assembly line has a stop cord: if any inspection fails, the car cannot roll off the line until it is fixed (a red CI check blocks the merge). Testing every car by full test drive would be far too slow, so most confidence comes from the cheap early checks.

commonMisconceptions.myth: If my unit tests pass, my pipeline is correct.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Unit tests only verify code logic on fixed fixtures; they cannot catch upstream source changes, schema drift, SQL dialect quirks, or data-quality violations. You also need integration tests against a real engine and data assertions on the actual output.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Testing against a real warehouse in CI is too slow and expensive to be practical.
commonMisconceptions.reality: With Slim CI (build only modified models and downstream, defer the rest), ephemeral PR schemas, and dependency caching, a warehouse test runs in minutes for a few cents; full rebuilds are the anti-pattern, not warehouse testing itself.

productionConsiderations.scalability: Keep CI fast as the project grows by using Slim CI (state:modified+) so only changed models and their descendants build, parallelizing with a job matrix, caching dependencies, and sharding large unit-test suites across runners.
productionConsiderations.reliability: Make tests deterministic and isolated - pin image tags, freeze time and seed randomness, give each test its own transaction or ephemeral schema, and mock external services - so a red build always means a real problem, not flakiness.
productionConsiderations.faultTolerance: Always tear down containers and ephemeral schemas in an 'if: always()' step so a failed test never leaks resources; retry only genuinely transient steps (image pulls, container readiness) with bounded backoff, never data assertions.
productionConsiderations.monitoring: Publish JUnit/HTML test reports and coverage as artifacts on every run, track test duration and flakiness over time, and alert when CI pass rates or run times degrade so the suite itself is observed.
productionConsiderations.security: Use short-lived, least-privilege warehouse credentials scoped to the ephemeral schema via GitHub Actions OIDC/secrets, never bake credentials into images or logs, and mask secrets in output so PR runs from forks cannot exfiltrate them.
productionConsiderations.costOptimization: Rebuild only changed models (Slim CI), tear down ephemeral schemas promptly, use a cheap engine (DuckDB) for integration tests where the warehouse dialect is not required, and cache aggressively to avoid repeated downloads and rebuilds.
productionConsiderations.performance: Order the pipeline fastest-to-slowest (lint -> unit -> integration -> warehouse -> E2E) with fail-fast so cheap checks catch most errors first, reuse warmed containers within a job, and keep fixtures small but representative.

codeExamples.title: GitHub Actions workflow: matrix, caching, dbt build in a sandbox schema, published report
codeExamples.overview: A pull-request CI workflow that lints and unit-tests across a Python matrix with dependency caching, provisions an ephemeral warehouse schema, runs 'dbt build' (models + data tests) into that sandbox, uploads a test report, and tears the schema down.
codeExamples.code:
name: pipeline-ci

on:
  pull_request:
    branches: [ main ]

concurrency:
  group: ci-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

jobs:
  unit:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        python-version: ["3.11", "3.12"]
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: ${{ matrix.python-version }}
          cache: pip
      - name: Install deps
        run: pip install -r requirements-dev.txt
      - name: Run unit tests
        run: pytest tests/unit -q --junitxml=report-${{ matrix.python-version }}.xml
      - name: Upload test report
        if: always()
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: unit-report-${{ matrix.python-version }}
          path: report-${{ matrix.python-version }}.xml

  dbt:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    needs: unit
    env:
      DBT_SCHEMA: dbt_ci_pr_${{ github.event.pull_request.number }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: "3.12"
          cache: pip
      - name: Install dbt
        run: pip install dbt-snowflake==1.8.*
      - name: Cache dbt packages
        uses: actions/cache@v4
        with:
          path: dbt_packages
          key: dbt-deps-${{ hashFiles('packages.yml') }}
      - name: dbt deps
        run: dbt deps
      - name: dbt build (Slim CI into sandbox schema)
        env:
          SNOWFLAKE_ACCOUNT: ${{ secrets.SNOWFLAKE_ACCOUNT }}
          SNOWFLAKE_USER: ${{ secrets.SNOWFLAKE_USER }}
          SNOWFLAKE_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.SNOWFLAKE_PASSWORD }}
        run: |
          dbt build --target ci \
            --select state:modified+ --defer --state ./prod-manifest
      - name: Upload dbt run results
        if: always()
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: dbt-run-results
          path: target/run_results.json
      - name: Drop ephemeral schema
        if: always()
        run: dbt run-operation drop_ci_schema --args "{schema: $DBT_SCHEMA}"
codeExamples.breakdown: 'on: pull_request' triggers the workflow per PR; 'concurrency' cancels superseded runs to save minutes. The 'unit' job uses a matrix over Python 3.11/3.12 (fail-fast:false so both report), 'cache: pip' restores the pip cache, and JUnit XML is uploaded as an artifact even on failure ('if: always()'). The 'dbt' job needs the unit job, sets an ephemeral schema name from the PR number, caches dbt packages by hashing packages.yml, and runs 'dbt build --select state:modified+ --defer --state ./prod-manifest' (Slim CI: only changed models + descendants, deferring unchanged refs to prod). run_results.json is published, and an always-run step drops the sandbox schema for cost control.
codeExamples.expectedOutput:
unit (3.11)   ✓ 42 passed in 3.1s
unit (3.12)   ✓ 42 passed in 3.0s
dbt           Running with dbt=1.8.7
              Found 6 modified models, 18 tests
              1 of 24 OK created sql table model dbt_ci_pr_1234.stg_orders ...
              24 of 24 PASS  ... [PASS in 47.2s]
              Completed successfully
              Done. PASS=24 WARN=0 ERROR=0 SKIP=0 TOTAL=24
codeExamples.commonIssues: Forgetting 'if: always()' so reports and schema teardown are skipped when tests fail (leaking schemas). Not restoring a production manifest, so 'state:modified+' selects nothing or everything. Exposing warehouse secrets to fork PRs. Cache key not including the lockfile hash, so stale dependencies are reused.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Use OIDC to assume a short-lived warehouse role instead of static secrets; add path filters so docs-only PRs skip the dbt job; store the prod manifest as a downloadable artifact from the main-branch build; run dbt with '--fail-fast' to stop on the first failing model.

codeExamples.title: pytest + testcontainers: integration test against a real Postgres with a fixture
codeExamples.overview: A pytest fixture boots a real, pinned Postgres in Docker via testcontainers, applies schema, and a test runs the pipeline's real transformation SQL and asserts on the result; the terminal output shows the run with coverage.
codeExamples.code:
# tests/integration/test_orders_pipeline.py
import pytest
from sqlalchemy import create_engine, text
from testcontainers.postgres import PostgresContainer
from pipeline.transform import build_daily_revenue


@pytest.fixture(scope="module")
def pg_engine():
    with PostgresContainer("postgres:16-alpine") as pg:
        engine = create_engine(pg.get_connection_url())
        with engine.begin() as c:
            c.execute(text(
                "CREATE TABLE orders (id INT, amount NUMERIC, status TEXT, ts TIMESTAMP)"
            ))
            c.execute(text(
                "INSERT INTO orders VALUES "
                "(1, 100, 'paid', '2026-01-01'), "
                "(2,  50, 'refunded', '2026-01-01'), "
                "(3, 200, 'paid', '2026-01-01')"
            ))
        yield engine


def test_daily_revenue_excludes_refunds(pg_engine):
    build_daily_revenue(pg_engine)  # runs the real pipeline SQL
    with pg_engine.connect() as c:
        rows = c.execute(text(
            "SELECT day, revenue FROM daily_revenue ORDER BY day"
        )).fetchall()
    assert rows == [("2026-01-01", 300)]  # 100 + 200, refund excluded


def test_daily_revenue_handles_empty(pg_engine):
    with pg_engine.begin() as c:
        c.execute(text("DELETE FROM orders"))
    build_daily_revenue(pg_engine)
    with pg_engine.connect() as c:
        n = c.execute(text("SELECT count(*) FROM daily_revenue")).scalar()
    assert n == 0

# Run: pytest tests/integration -q --cov=pipeline
codeExamples.breakdown: The module-scoped 'pg_engine' fixture starts a pinned postgres:16-alpine container (testcontainers waits until it accepts connections), creates a SQLAlchemy engine, applies DDL, and seeds three orders - one refunded. 'yield' hands the engine to tests; the 'with' block guarantees the container is stopped and removed on teardown. 'test_daily_revenue_excludes_refunds' runs the real 'build_daily_revenue' transformation and asserts refunds are excluded (300, not 350). The second test proves the empty-input edge case. Because a genuine Postgres runs the SQL, dialect and numeric behavior are exactly production's.

codeExamples.commonIssues: Docker not available on the runner (testcontainers needs a Docker daemon). Using 'postgres:latest' instead of a pinned tag, breaking reproducibility. Function-scoped container per test making the suite slow. Not cleaning state between tests, so ordering causes false failures. Forgetting to wait for readiness on slower engines.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Use module or session scope to reuse one container across tests and roll back per test in a transaction for isolation; use postgres:16-alpine for faster pulls; swap to an in-process DuckDB when warehouse dialect parity is not required; cache the Docker image layer in CI to cut startup time.

endToEndExample.businessProblem: An e-commerce analytics team ships changes to their dbt models several times a day. Twice last quarter a refactor silently double-counted refunded orders, inflating the executive revenue dashboard for three days before finance caught it. They want every pull request to automatically prove that transformation logic is correct and that the output data satisfies quality contracts, in a sandbox, before merge - without rebuilding the whole warehouse each time.
endToEndExample.inputData: A monorepo with a Python ingestion package (pipeline/), a dbt project (models/staging + models/marts including daily_revenue), pytest suites (tests/unit, tests/integration), dbt schema tests (unique, not_null, relationships, accepted_values), a stored production manifest for Slim CI, and a GitHub Actions workflow. Source data is raw orders and refunds in the warehouse.
endToEndExample.architecture: PR opened -> GitHub Actions (pull_request) -> job 1 lint + pytest unit (matrix 3.11/3.12, pip cache) -> job 2 pytest integration with testcontainers Postgres -> job 3 provision ephemeral schema dbt_ci_pr_N -> dbt deps (cached) -> dbt build --select state:modified+ --defer --state ./prod-manifest into the sandbox -> upload JUnit + run_results.json artifacts -> required status checks gate merge -> always-run teardown drops the ephemeral schema.
processingSteps: 1. A developer edits the daily_revenue model and opens a PR; GitHub Actions triggers, checks out the commit, and restores the pip and dbt package caches.
2. The unit job runs pytest across Python 3.11 and 3.12 in parallel, verifying pure transform functions (refund exclusion, rounding, dedup) in seconds.

3. The integration job boots a pinned Postgres via testcontainers, seeds orders and refunds, runs the real load-and-transform code, and asserts the resulting tables are correct, then tears the container down.

4. A step provisions the ephemeral schema dbt_ci_pr_1234 and runs 'dbt build --select state:modified+ --defer', materializing only the changed models and descendants and executing their schema/data tests (unique order_id, not_null revenue, refunds relationship) in that isolated sandbox.
5. JUnit XML and run_results.json are uploaded as PR artifacts, required checks turn green or red to gate the merge, and an 'if: always()' step drops dbt_ci_pr_1234 so no warehouse cost lingers.
endToEndExample.output: A pull request annotated with green (or red) status checks, a downloadable test report showing unit/integration results with coverage and a dbt summary (PASS=24 WARN=0 ERROR=0), the changed models materialized and validated only in a throwaway schema, and production untouched. Merge is blocked unless every required check passes.
endToEndExample.monitoring: The workflow publishes test reports and coverage on every run; a dashboard tracks CI pass rate, average run duration, and per-test flakiness. Alerts fire if the pass rate drops or the dbt CI run time regresses, and run_results.json feeds a check on model-build timing.
endToEndExample.errorHandling: Transient failures (image pull, container readiness) retry with bounded backoff; data assertion failures never retry - they fail the check with the offending rows in the report. An 'if: always()' teardown step drops the ephemeral schema and removes containers even when tests fail, so a red build never leaks resources or cost.
endToEndExample.finalResult: The double-counting class of bug is now caught on the PR: the dbt 'unique' and refunds-relationship tests fail in the sandbox before merge, the author sees the failing rows in the report, fixes the join, and only then can merge. Warehouse cost stays negligible because Slim CI rebuilds just the changed models and the schema is dropped afterward, and the executive dashboard has not had a silent revenue error since.

industryUseCases.company: A fintech analytics-engineering team on Snowflake + dbt
industryUseCases.problem: Dozens of analysts change hundreds of dbt models weekly; full warehouse rebuilds in CI were too slow and costly, and untested changes occasionally broke regulatory reports.
industryUseCases.solution: Slim CI in GitHub Actions builds only 'state:modified+' models into a per-PR ephemeral schema with deferral to production, runs dbt schema/data tests plus dbt_expectations checks, and gates merge on required status checks; schemas are dropped on close.
industryUseCases.benefits: CI runs dropped from over an hour to a few minutes at a fraction of the cost, regulatory-report regressions are caught on the PR, and analysts merge with confidence.

industryUseCases.company: A logistics platform team building Python + Airflow pipelines
industryUseCases.problem: ETL bugs (timezone handling, SQL dialect quirks, constraint violations) only surfaced in production because tests used mocks that hid real database behavior.
industryUseCases.solution: pytest with testcontainers spins up the exact Postgres version used in production for integration tests, plus fast unit tests for pure functions and Great Expectations checks on outputs, all run in GitHub Actions with caching and a matrix.
industryUseCases.benefits: Dialect and constraint bugs are now caught in CI against a real engine, production incidents from ETL regressions fell sharply, and refactors are safe.

industryUseCases.company: A media company's ML feature-engineering group
industryUseCases.problem: Feature pipelines feeding models drifted silently - schema changes and null spikes corrupted features and degraded model performance before anyone noticed.
industryUseCases.solution: Data contracts and Great Expectations/Pandera suites validate schema, null rates, and value ranges in CI on ephemeral compute, with snapshot/golden tests on representative feature batches and merge gating on the checks.
industryUseCases.benefits: Silent feature drift is caught before merge, model-performance regressions traced to bad features dropped, and data scientists trust the feature store.

productionDeepDive.scalability: The suite scales with the project by building only changed dbt models and their descendants (Slim CI state:modified+ --defer), sharding and parallelizing unit tests across a runner matrix, caching dependencies and dbt packages, and reserving slow end-to-end tests for a nightly or pre-release run rather than every PR.
productionDeepDive.faultTolerance: Every resource is torn down in an 'if: always()' step so failures never leak containers or ephemeral schemas; only genuinely transient steps (image pulls, container readiness, network) retry with bounded backoff, while data and logic assertions fail immediately and loudly.
productionDeepDive.highAvailability: CI is treated as production infrastructure: pinned action and image versions prevent surprise breakage, a fallback runner pool or self-hosted runners absorb capacity spikes, and the workflow is itself tested (a canary PR) so onboarding and the gate never silently rot.
productionDeepDive.disasterRecovery: The production manifest and pinned image/dependency versions are the recovery source of truth for reproducing any CI run; ephemeral schemas and containers are disposable by design, so a corrupted test environment is simply recreated from the pinned definitions on the next run.
productionDeepDive.performanceOptimization: Order jobs fastest-to-slowest with fail-fast (lint -> unit -> integration -> dbt -> E2E), reuse a warmed container per module and roll back per test, cache pip/uv and dbt_packages by lockfile hash, use DuckDB for integration tests where warehouse dialect parity is not needed, and cancel superseded runs via concurrency groups.
productionDeepDive.costOptimization: Rebuild only modified models, drop ephemeral schemas promptly, prefer in-process DuckDB over spinning warehouse compute when possible, skip heavy jobs on docs-only PRs via path filters, and use concurrency cancellation so pushes don't stack up billable minutes.
productionDeepDive.securityConsiderations: Authenticate to the warehouse with short-lived OIDC-assumed roles scoped to the ephemeral schema rather than static secrets, mask secrets in logs, restrict secret access from fork PRs (pull_request_target hygiene), use least-privilege CI credentials, and never bake credentials into container images.
productionDeepDive.monitoringAndObservability: Publish JUnit/HTML reports, coverage, and dbt run_results.json as artifacts on every run; track pass rate, run duration, and flaky-test frequency on a dashboard; alert when the gate's pass rate or latency degrades so the health of the test system itself is visible.
productionDeepDive.dataQualityValidation: Enforce explicit contracts in CI - dbt tests (unique, not_null, relationships, accepted_values), dbt_expectations/Great Expectations for distributions and ranges, freshness and row-count/volume anomaly checks - so the actual output data, not just the code, must satisfy the contract before merge.
productionDeepDive.loggingAndAlerting: Each job logs its stage and command clearly; failing assertions surface the offending rows/values in the report and PR summary; CI posts a status back to the PR, and integrations (Slack/GitHub checks) alert the author on failure while blocking merge until the pipeline is green.

recommendedPractices: **Follow the pyramid:** many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests against a real containerized engine, targeted data-quality assertions, and only a handful of end-to-end tests.
**Test code and data:** pair pytest logic tests with dbt/Great Expectations data contracts so both wrong logic and bad data fail the build.
**Use ephemeral, isolated environments:** run each PR against its own container or sandbox schema and always tear it down, never against shared or production data.
**Gate the merge:** make the CI checks required in branch protection so a red pipeline cannot be merged, and keep the suite fast enough that no one is tempted to skip it.
engineeringStandards: Pin every image, action, and dependency version so CI runs are reproducible and don't break on upstream changes.
Make tests deterministic: freeze time, seed randomness, mock external systems, and isolate state per test.
Run the same checks locally (pre-commit / make test) as in CI so developers get feedback before pushing.
designRecommendations: Separate tests into tests/unit, tests/integration, and dbt tests so each layer can run and scale independently.
Adopt Slim CI (state:modified+ --defer) with a stored production manifest so warehouse builds test only what changed.
Keep fixtures small but representative, and use golden/snapshot files for wide outputs instead of exhaustive per-field asserts.
namingConventions: Name ephemeral schemas by PR (e.g. dbt_ci_pr_1234) so they are traceable and easy to drop.
Use clear test names that describe behavior (test_daily_revenue_excludes_refunds) rather than the function under test.
Prefix CI-only dbt targets and profiles ('ci') to keep them distinct from dev and prod.
documentationStandards: Document how to run each test layer locally and what infrastructure (Docker) it requires in the README/CONTRIBUTING.
Describe every data contract (which tests guard which model and why) so the intent behind assertions is clear.
Document the Slim CI setup, required secrets/OIDC roles, and the teardown behavior so the pipeline is maintainable.
testingStrategies: Run lint and unit tests on every push; run integration, dbt build, and data tests on every PR; reserve full end-to-end runs for nightly or pre-release.
Parametrize unit tests over edge cases (nulls, empties, duplicates, timezone boundaries) and use factory/faker data for volume.
Verify the CI path end to end periodically with a canary PR so the gate and teardown never silently break.

commonMistakes.mistake: Relying only on unit tests with mocked databases and no real-engine or data-quality checks.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Mocks are fast and easy to write, and unit tests feel like sufficient coverage, so teams skip the harder integration and data layers.
commonMistakes.impact: Dialect quirks, constraint violations, schema drift, and data-contract breaches slip through to production because nothing ever exercised the real engine or the actual output data.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Add integration tests with testcontainers against the real engine and data assertions (dbt/Great Expectations) on outputs, keeping mocks only for truly external third-party services.

commonMistakes.mistake: Rebuilding the entire warehouse on every pull request.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: It is the simplest thing to configure ('dbt build' with no selection) and guarantees everything is tested, so teams start there and never optimize.
commonMistakes.impact: CI runs take an hour or more and cost significant warehouse compute, so developers wait, batch changes, or pressure to disable the checks.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Use Slim CI ('dbt build --select state:modified+ --defer --state ./prod-manifest') with a stored production manifest so only changed models and their descendants build into an ephemeral schema.

commonMistakes.mistake: Leaving ephemeral schemas and containers behind after tests, and letting tests be non-deterministic.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Teardown is added as a normal step (skipped on failure) and tests depend on time/order/shared state without anyone noticing until CI is flaky.
commonMistakes.impact: Abandoned schemas accumulate warehouse cost, and flaky red builds train the team to ignore failures, defeating the entire purpose of gating.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Tear down in an 'if: always()' step, freeze time and seed randomness, isolate state per test (transaction or fresh schema), and pin all versions so a red build always means a real defect.

comparisonSection.explanation: A mocked database is instant and dependency-free, but it only returns what you told it to, so it cannot catch SQL dialect differences, constraint enforcement, transaction semantics, or type coercion - the very bugs integration tests exist to find. testcontainers boots the real, pinned engine (the same Postgres/MySQL version as production) in Docker for the test and tears it down afterward, giving true fidelity at the cost of Docker availability and a few seconds of startup. Use mocks for genuinely external third-party APIs; use testcontainers (or an in-process DuckDB when dialect parity isn't required) for anything that runs real SQL, so tests reflect how the pipeline actually behaves.

dbt tests are ideal when your transformations already live in dbt: they are terse YAML (unique, not_null, relationships, accepted_values, plus dbt_utils/dbt_expectations), version-controlled beside the models, and run naturally in 'dbt build'. Great Expectations is a standalone, framework-agnostic data-quality tool with a rich library of expectations, profiling, and human-readable Data Docs, better suited to validating data outside dbt (e.g. Python/Spark pipelines, files, or arbitrary sources) and to richer statistical/distributional checks. Many teams use dbt tests for warehouse models and Great Expectations (or Soda/Pandera) for ingestion and non-dbt pipelines; the choice follows where the data lives and how expressive the assertions must be.

beginnerQuestions.question: What is the difference between testing the code and testing the data in a pipeline?
beginnerQuestions.answer: Testing the code (unit/integration tests) verifies that your transformation logic computes the correct output for given input - it fails when logic regresses. Testing the data (data-quality assertions like dbt tests or Great Expectations) verifies that the actual data flowing through satisfies a contract - not_null, unique, valid ranges, freshness - and can fail even when the code is correct because an upstream source changed. A reliable pipeline needs both.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: Interviewers want to hear that you distinguish logic correctness from data validity and know that unit tests alone cannot catch upstream data problems.

beginnerQuestions.question: What is the testing pyramid and how does it apply to data pipelines?
beginnerQuestions.answer: The pyramid prescribes many cheap, fast unit tests at the base, fewer integration tests in the middle, and only a small number of slow end-to-end tests at the top; for data you also add a layer of data-quality assertions. It keeps CI fast and stable because most feedback comes from millisecond unit tests, while expensive and flaky-prone end-to-end tests are kept rare.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: Show you understand the cost/speed/fidelity trade-off and would not build a top-heavy suite of slow E2E tests.

intermediateQuestions.question: How do testcontainers make integration tests more reliable than mocks?
intermediateQuestions.answer: testcontainers starts a real, pinned database (the same version as production) in a throwaway Docker container for the test, yields a connection to it, and tears it down afterward. Because the test runs real SQL against the real engine, it catches dialect differences, constraint enforcement, transaction behavior, and type coercion that a mock - which only returns canned values - cannot. It gives production fidelity without a shared, manually managed test database.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Mention pinning the image tag, using a pytest fixture, readiness waiting, and reusing one container per module with per-test rollback for speed.

intermediateQuestions.question: What is Slim CI in dbt and why does it matter?
intermediateQuestions.answer: Slim CI runs 'dbt build --select state:modified+ --defer --state ./prod-manifest': it compares the PR against a stored production manifest and rebuilds only modified models and everything downstream, deferring unchanged upstream references to existing production tables instead of rebuilding them. This turns a multi-hour full warehouse build into a few-minute targeted build, making warehouse testing in CI fast and cost-effective.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Emphasize the stored manifest (state), the '+' selecting descendants (blast radius), '--defer', and the ephemeral PR schema.

advancedQuestions.question: How do you keep a data-pipeline CI suite fast and cheap as the project scales to thousands of models?
advancedQuestions.answer: Build only what changed with Slim CI (state:modified+ --defer) into an ephemeral per-PR schema; parallelize and shard unit tests across a runner matrix; cache dependencies and dbt packages by lockfile hash; use in-process DuckDB for integration tests where warehouse dialect isn't required; reserve full end-to-end/full-refresh runs for nightly or pre-release; and use concurrency cancellation and path filters to avoid wasted minutes. Always tear down ephemeral resources to control cost.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Demonstrate the concrete levers - selective builds, caching, parallelism, cheaper engines, scheduling heavy tests off the PR path - and cost discipline via teardown.

advancedQuestions.question: How do you prevent flaky tests from undermining a merge-gating CI pipeline?
advancedQuestions.answer: Eliminate the two root causes: non-determinism (freeze time with freezegun, seed randomness, mock or containerize network dependencies, avoid order-dependent assertions) and lack of isolation (each test gets its own transaction or ephemeral schema and cleans up). Pin all image/action/dependency versions, retry only genuinely transient infrastructure steps (image pull, container readiness) with bounded backoff - never data assertions - and monitor flaky-test frequency so regressions in stability are visible.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Show that trust in the gate depends on determinism and isolation, and that retries must never mask real assertion failures.

scenarioBasedQuestions.scenario: A refactor of a dbt model silently double-counts refunded orders, inflating the revenue dashboard for three days before finance notices. Design CI so this class of bug is caught before merge.
scenarioBasedQuestions.thinkingProcess: The bug is a logic error producing contract-plausible-but-wrong data, so I need layers that would catch it: unit tests on the refund-exclusion logic, an integration/dbt test asserting the numeric result, and data contracts (unique order_id, refunds relationship) that fail when double-counting duplicates rows. It must run per PR against an isolated sandbox and gate the merge.
scenarioBasedQuestions.expectedAnswer: Add a pytest unit test that feeds a paid and a refunded order and asserts refunds are excluded; add a dbt/integration test on daily_revenue asserting the expected total; add dbt data tests - 'unique' on the grain and a 'relationships' test to the refunds table - which fail when the join duplicates rows. Run all of this in GitHub Actions via Slim CI into an ephemeral schema (dbt_ci_pr_N), publish the report, and make the checks required in branch protection so the failing assertion blocks merge, with the offending rows visible to the author. Add a nightly full-refresh run as a backstop.

systemDesignQuestions.problemStatement: Design a CI testing system for a 40-person analytics-engineering team with a large dbt project on a cloud warehouse, where changes must be validated per PR without rebuilding the whole warehouse or touching production.
systemDesignQuestions.designApproach: In GitHub Actions on pull_request: job 1 lints and runs pytest unit tests across a Python matrix with pip caching; job 2 runs pytest integration tests via testcontainers (or DuckDB) against real SQL; job 3 provisions an ephemeral per-PR schema, runs 'dbt build --select state:modified+ --defer --state ./prod-manifest' (models + schema/data tests) using a manifest published by the main-branch build, and adds Great Expectations checks for ingestion. Publish JUnit/run_results artifacts, gate merge on required status checks via branch protection, authenticate with short-lived OIDC warehouse roles, and drop the ephemeral schema in an 'if: always()' teardown.
systemDesignQuestions.tradeOffs: Slim CI is fast and cheap but depends on a fresh, correct production manifest; testcontainers give real fidelity but need Docker on runners and add startup time (DuckDB is faster but not always dialect-identical). More data contracts increase confidence but add maintenance and can be noisy. Merge gating enforces quality but requires the suite to stay fast or developers will resist it.
systemDesignQuestions.scalingStrategy: Keep per-PR cost roughly constant with selective builds, caching, parallel matrices, and sharded unit tests; publish the prod manifest as an artifact and refresh it on each main build; move full-refresh and heavy E2E tests to nightly; use concurrency cancellation and path filters to trim wasted minutes; and monitor CI duration, pass rate, and flakiness to catch degradation early.

cheatSheet.oneLineDefinition: Testing data pipelines in CI is an automated, layered suite - unit tests for transform logic, integration tests against a real containerized engine, dbt/Great Expectations data-quality contracts, and a few end-to-end runs in ephemeral per-PR environments - all run on every pull request and gating the merge.
keyConcepts: Testing pyramid: many unit tests, fewer integration tests, targeted data tests, few E2E tests - keep it fast and stable.
Test code AND data: pytest for logic, dbt/Great Expectations/Soda for data contracts (nulls, uniqueness, freshness, ranges).
Real engines via testcontainers (or DuckDB) beat mocks for catching dialect/constraint/transaction bugs.
Slim CI: 'dbt build --select state:modified+ --defer' builds only changed models into an ephemeral per-PR schema.
Determinism + isolation + always-teardown + merge gating make a red build trustworthy and cheap.
commands: pytest tests/unit -q --junitxml=report.xml   # fast unit tests with a JUnit report
pytest tests/integration -q --cov=pipeline   # integration tests (testcontainers) with coverage
dbt deps   # install dbt packages (cache dbt_packages in CI)
dbt build --target ci --select state:modified+ --defer --state ./prod-manifest   # Slim CI
dbt test --select orders   # run data-quality tests for a model
great_expectations checkpoint run daily_revenue   # run a GX expectation suite
soda scan -d warehouse checks.yml   # run Soda data checks
gh pr checks   # view required status checks on the PR
docker compose -f compose.ci.yaml up -d   # start pinned local services for integration tests
interviewPoints: Distinguish testing code (logic) from testing data (contracts) - you need both layers.
The pyramid keeps CI fast: most confidence from unit tests, E2E kept rare.
testcontainers run the real pinned engine so dialect/constraint bugs are caught, unlike mocks.
Slim CI (state:modified+ --defer) plus ephemeral schemas make warehouse testing fast and cheap.
Determinism, isolation, always-teardown, and required checks are what make merge gating work.
quickNotes: Pin image/action/dependency versions - never ':latest' - for reproducible CI.
Tear down containers and ephemeral schemas in an 'if: always()' step to avoid leaked cost.
Cache pip/uv and dbt_packages by lockfile hash; use a matrix and fail-fast ordering.
Use OIDC short-lived warehouse roles; restrict secrets from fork PRs.
Reserve full-refresh and heavy end-to-end tests for nightly, not every PR.

keyTakeaways: Test both the code and the data: pair pytest logic tests with data-quality contracts (dbt tests, Great Expectations, Soda) so wrong logic and bad data both fail the build.

Follow the testing pyramid - many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests against a real containerized engine (testcontainers/DuckDB), targeted data assertions, and only a few end-to-end tests - to keep CI fast and trustworthy.

Use Slim CI ('dbt build --select state:modified+ --defer' with a stored production manifest) into ephemeral per-PR schemas so warehouse testing runs in minutes for cents instead of rebuilding everything.

Make tests deterministic and isolated, tear down containers and ephemeral schemas in an 'if: always()' step, and pin every version so a red build always signals a real defect, not flakiness or leaked cost.

Orchestrate it all in GitHub Actions with a matrix, dependency caching, published test reports, and required status checks in branch protection so a failing check blocks the merge before anything reaches production.
